file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below are two ways you can launch a **Google Cloud Compute Engine** instance that has an **NVIDIA RTX A6000** GPU and runs **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS**.

> ⚠️ **Prerequisites**  
> * You must have a Google Cloud project with the **Compute Engine API** enabled.  
> * You need a GPU‑enabled zone (e.g., `us-central1-b`, `us-east1-c`, etc.).  
> * Your account must have the **GPU quota** for the chosen zone.  
> * The **NVIDIA driver** will be installed automatically if you use the `--guest-os-features=enable-nvidia-driver` flag (or you can install it manually later).  

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Replace PROJECT_ID, ZONE, and INSTANCE_NAME with your own values
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-b"
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"

gcloud compute instances create $INSTANCE_NAME \
    --project=$PROJECT_ID \
    --zone=$ZONE \
    --machine-type=n1-standard-8 \          # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM (adjust as needed)
    --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1 \
    --image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size=100GB \
    --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
    --boot-disk-device-name=$INSTANCE_NAME \
    --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
    --restart-on-failure \
    --guest-os-features=enable-nvidia-driver \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh   # optional: custom init script
```

### Explanation of key flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM configuration. `n1-standard-8` gives 8 vCPUs & 30 GB RAM. |
| `--accelerator` | Adds the GPU. `type=nvidia-tesla-a6000` specifies the RTX A6000. |
| `--image-family` / `--image-project` | Pulls the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image from the official Ubuntu Cloud image project. |
| `--boot-disk-size` | Size of the boot disk. |
| `--guest-os-features=enable-nvidia-driver` | Installs the NVIDIA driver automatically during boot. |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script` | Optional: run a shell script at first boot (e.g., to install CUDA, set up environment). |

> **Tip:** If you prefer a different machine type (e.g., `n1-highmem-16`), just change the `--machine-type` value.

---

## 2. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine API directly (e.g., from a script or a CI/CD pipeline), you can POST a JSON payload to the `instances.insert` endpoint.

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-b/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "zones/us-central1-b/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorType": "projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-b/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a6000",
      "acceleratorCount": 1
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": [
        "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "guest-os-features",
        "value": "enable-nvidia-driver"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### How to call it

```bash
# Assuming you have a valid OAuth 2.0 access token in $ACCESS_TOKEN
curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @instance.json \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-b/instances"
```

Replace:

* `my-gcp-project` with your project ID.
* `us-central1-b` with your chosen zone.
* `instance.json` with the path to the JSON file above.

---

## 3. Quick sanity check

After the instance is running, you can SSH into it and verify the GPU:

```bash
ssh rtx-a6000-ubuntu@<external-ip>
nvidia-smi
```

You should see the RTX A6000 listed with its driver version.

---

### Common pitfalls

| Issue | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| **Quota exceeded** | Request a GPU quota increase in the GCP console. |
| **Instance fails to start** | Ensure the zone supports GPUs (`gcloud compute zones list --filter='supportsAccelerators:true'`). |
| **Driver not installed** | Add `--guest-os-features=enable-nvidia-driver` or install manually via `sudo apt-get install nvidia-driver-470`. |

Feel free to tweak the machine type, disk size, or add additional metadata items (e.g., startup scripts) to suit your workload. Happy computing!
